summary: A full, timed EST I English practice test: Literacy Test 1 (Writing and Language, 44 questions, 35 minutes) and Literacy Test 2 (Reading, 52 questions, 65 minutes), with an explanation for every answer.

blocks.text: This is a complete practice version of the two English parts of EST I: **Literacy Test 1 (Writing and Language)** and **Literacy Test 2 (Reading)**. Every passage and question was written for this site by Mohamed Abdelkriem. The test is modelled on the skills that the EST Literacy tests measure; it is not made of official EST questions, and the real test may present questions in a different way.

rows: Four essays with numbered, underlined parts. Fix grammar and punctuation, and improve transitions, order, wording and relevance.
Five long passages (fiction set in a city, humanities, science with a table, a pair of opinion texts, science). Answer questions about ideas, details, words, structure, evidence and data.

blocks.text: These figures are as published by schools; check the latest official EST candidate guide on est.moe.gov.eg before your test.

items: Sit in a quiet place with no phone, no dictionary and no help, exactly as in the real test.
Do the two sections in one sitting if you can. The timer starts when you begin each section and the section ends when the time is up.
Work through the questions in order. You can mark a question and come back to it while the section is still open, but once a section ends you cannot return to it, just as in the real test.
Answer every question. A blank is always wrong; a careful guess may be right.

Each passage is repeated above each of its questions. In Literacy Test 1, only the part that question asks about is underlined and numbered. In Literacy Test 2, the paragraphs are numbered [1], [2], [3] so that questions can point to them.
At the end you see a practice percentage for each section. It is not an official EST scaled score; use it to measure your progress from one practice test to the next.

questions.p:
**Satellites the Size of a Shoebox**
For most of the space age, building a satellite was a job for governments and giant companies. A single spacecraft could take ten years to design and cost hundreds of millions of dollars. Today, __[1] for example,__ some satellites are small enough to hold in two hands, and university students build them.
These tiny spacecraft are called CubeSats. The basic unit is a cube ten centimetres on each side. Larger CubeSats made by joining several units together. Because every CubeSat follows the same standard size, it can be loaded into a common launcher and carried into orbit alongside a much larger satellite. This shared ride make launching far cheaper than sending a spacecraft up on its own rocket.
Inside the small box, engineers must fit everything a satellite needs; solar cells to collect energy, a battery, a radio, and a computer to control it all. Many teams use parts originally designed for mobile phones, which are light, cheap and tested by millions of users. Space, however, is harsh. Without air to carry heat away, electronics can overheat and become too hot in sunlight and freeze in shadow, and radiation can scramble a computers' memory.
Despite these difficulties, CubeSats have done some pretty awesome stuff. They have photographed farmland to help farmers track their crops, measured the thin upper atmosphere, and they were testing new technologies before those technologies will be trusted on larger missions. For students, the greatest value may be the experience itself. A team that has designed, built and tested a working satellite has learned lessons that no textbook can teach.
The small size of CubeSats does create one serious problem. Thousands of satellites are now circling the Earth, and each new one adds to the risk of collisions. Engineers are therefore designing CubeSats that fall back into the atmosphere and burn up within a few years of finishing their work. Small satellites, in other words, must also leave space as tidy as they found it.
questions.q: [1] Which choice provides the most logical transition?
c: NO CHANGE
similarly,
however,
therefore,
questions.e: The sentence contrasts the past (only governments and giant companies built satellites) with today (students build tiny ones), so the contrast word "however" is needed. "Therefore" wrongly presents today's small satellites as a result of the old, expensive ones.
ce: Today's tiny satellites are not an example of the costly spacecraft just described; they are the opposite.
"Similarly" signals likeness, but the two sentences describe a big difference.
Correct: the sentence contrasts the expensive past with the cheaper present.
Small student satellites are not a result of governments building expensive ones.

questions.p:
**The Fish That Makes Beaches**
Visitors who snorkel over the coral reefs of the Red Sea often hear a strange sound under the water__[12]: a steady__ crunching, like someone eating crisps. The noise comes from parrotfish brightly coloured fish named for the beak-like plates of teeth at the front of their mouths.
Parrotfish feed mainly on algae, the tiny plants that grow on rocks and dead coral. To reach them, the hard surface is scraped by a parrotfish's beak, swallowing pieces of rock and coral along with its meal. A second set of teeth in its throat then grind this material into fine grains. The fish digests the algae and passes the rest out of its body as white sand.
The amount of sand is surprising. Some scientists estimate that a single large parrotfish can produce hundreds of kilograms of sand in a year. Sand can also be made into glass when it is heated to a very high temperature. On some tropical islands, much of the white sand on the beaches was produced in this way.
Parrotfish matter to the reef for another reason. Algae grow quickly, and if nothing eats them, they can spread over the coral and block the sunlight that corals need. By grazing every day on a daily basis, parrotfish keep the algae under control and leave clean surfaces where young corals can settle and grow. However, many marine biologists describe parrotfish as the gardeners of the reef.
Some parrotfish also have an unusual habit at night, before sleeping, they wrap themselves in a bubble of mucus that they produce from their own bodies. Scientists believe this covering hides their scent from predators such as moray eels.
Because parrotfish protect the reef, divers and fishermen along the Egyptian coast has good reason to value them. A healthy population of these noisy grazers helps to keep the reefs colourful and the beaches white.

**Windows That Breathe**
Walk through the older streets of Cairo, and you may notice wooden screens __[23] jutting out and projecting outward from__ the upper floors of the houses. Made from hundreds of small turned pieces of wood fitted together into delicate patterns these screens are called mashrabiyas. For centuries, they were a common feature of homes across Egypt and much of the Islamic world.
A mashrabiya did several jobs at once. Its first purpose was to control the light. In a hot country, strong sunlight can make a room unbearable; the lattice broke the light into small patches, softening the glare while still letting people see out. Its second purpose was to cool the air. Breezes passed easy through the gaps in the wood, and in some houses, jars of water were placed in the screen so that the air moving over them was cooled.
The screens also protected privacy. People inside could look out at the busy street without being seen, an important consideration in a crowded city where houses stood close together.
Building a mashrabiya demanded great skill. Craftsmen shaped each wooden piece on a lathe, then joining the pieces without nails or glue, fitting them together so that the whole screen held their own shape. Because the joints allowed the wood to expand and shrink with changes in temperature without cracking, a well-made screen, could last for hundreds of years.
In the twentieth century, many mashrabiyas were removed as glass windows and electric fans became popular. Today, therefore, architects are taking a fresh look at them. In an age of rising temperatures and expensive energy, a screen that shades a room and lets the wind through without using any electricity seems less like an old-fashioned decoration and more like a super cool hack for the future.

**The Book Stall on the Corniche**
Every Friday morning during the summer I turned fourteen, my uncle Sherif __[34] wakes__ me before eight o'clock and took me to his book stall near the corniche in Alexandria. Alexandria was founded by Alexander the Great in the fourth century BC. The stall was little more than a long wooden table under a faded green umbrella but, it held hundreds of second-hand books stacked in leaning towers. My job, which was the task given to me, was to sort them.
For instance, I hated the work. The books smelled of dust and old paper, and the sea wind kept blowing the price tags away. Customers asked me for titles I had never heard of, and I had to call my uncle; who always knew exactly where each book was hidden. I could not understand how he remembered them all.
One morning, an elderly man in a grey suit stopped at the table and asked whether us had a book of poems by a writer whose name I did not recognise. Before I could call my uncle, I noticed a thin blue volume at the bottom of a pile. I pulled it out slowly, so that the tower above it would not fall. It was the book he wanted.
Holding the book with both hands, its pages were turned slowly by the man, as though they might tear. He told me that he had owned the same edition as a student, decades earlier and had lost it when his family moved house. He paid for it and then stood for a long time at the edge of the pavement, reading, while cars and bicycles passed behind him.
After that, I started looking for a different summer job. Each one had belonged to someone, and each one might be waiting for someone else. By the end of the summer, I could find most titles without asking my uncle, and I had started reading some of them myself. My uncle never said much about the change, but on the last Friday of the holiday he handed me the key to the stall's padlock and let me open up on my own.

Every Friday morning during the summer I turned fourteen, my uncle Sherif wakes me before eight o'clock and took me to his book stall near the corniche in Alexandria. Alexandria was founded by Alexander the Great in the fourth century BC. The stall was little more than a long wooden table under a faded green umbrella but, it held hundreds of second-hand books stacked in leaning towers. My job, which was the task given to me, was to sort them.
For instance, I hated the work. The books smelled of dust and old paper, and the sea wind kept blowing the price tags away. Customers asked me for titles I had never heard of, and I had to call my uncle; who always knew exactly where each book was hidden. I could not understand how he remembered them all.
One morning, an elderly man in a grey suit stopped at the table and asked whether __[40] us__ had a book of poems by a writer whose name I did not recognise. Before I could call my uncle, I noticed a thin blue volume at the bottom of a pile. I pulled it out slowly, so that the tower above it would not fall. It was the book he wanted.
Holding the book with both hands, its pages were turned slowly by the man, as though they might tear. He told me that he had owned the same edition as a student, decades earlier and had lost it when his family moved house. He paid for it and then stood for a long time at the edge of the pavement, reading, while cars and bicycles passed behind him.
After that, I started looking for a different summer job. Each one had belonged to someone, and each one might be waiting for someone else. By the end of the summer, I could find most titles without asking my uncle, and I had started reading some of them myself. My uncle never said much about the change, but on the last Friday of the holiday he handed me the key to the stall's padlock and let me open up on my own.

c: NO CHANGE
ours
ourselves
we

ce: "Us" is an object pronoun, but this word is the subject of "had".
"Ours" is a possessive pronoun and does not fit before "had a book".
"Ourselves" cannot be the subject of a verb.
Correct: "we" is the subject of "had".

questions.p:
**Passage 1 (Literary fiction).** This passage is adapted from an original short story. Nour, aged twelve, and her family have recently moved from a village in the Nile Delta to an apartment in Cairo.
**The Roof**
[1] From the window of the new apartment, Nour could see only other windows. They rose on every side like the walls of a well, five and six storeys of them, hung with washing and shuttered against the afternoon heat, and between them ran a strip of sky so narrow that a pigeon could cross it in two wingbeats. In the village there had been sky enough for a thousand pigeons. There had been the canal, and the mango trees behind her grandfather's house, and the fields that turned from green to gold and back again as reliably as the moon changed its face. Here there was concrete, and the sound of horns, and a smell of exhaust that settled on everything like fine grey flour.
[2] Her mother said she would grow used to it. Her father, who had taken the job at the printing works that had brought them all to the city, said nothing, but he came home each evening with ink in the creases of his hands and an expression that made Nour decide not to complain aloud. She complained instead to the window, silently, and the window, being a window, did not reply.
[3] It was the caretaker's boy who told her about the roof. Anyone could go up, he said, though most people did not bother, except for old Ustaz Ramzi, who had been a teacher of geography before his retirement and who now, according to the boy, spent his days among "his tins." Nour did not know what this meant and did not much care. But on the third Friday, when the apartment had grown so hot that even her mother had stopped pretending it was bearable, she climbed the last flight of stairs and pushed open the iron door.
[4] The light struck her first, then the green. Along the low wall that edged the roof stood a long row of containers: olive-oil tins, cracked buckets, a child's bathtub, half a dozen clay pots, each one full of earth and each one bursting with growth. There was mint, and basil, and a tomato plant tied to a broom handle; there were beans climbing a ladder of string; in one corner a small lemon tree stood in a barrel, holding out three hard green fruits as though it were offering them for inspection.
[5] Among the tins, with a watering can in his hand, stood an old man in a vest and a straw hat. He looked at her without surprise.
[6] "You are the new family on the fifth floor," he said. It was not a question. "You have come from the countryside. I can see it."
[7] Nour, who had been told many times not to be rude to her elders, was nonetheless rude. "How?" she said. "Do I look like a farmer?"
[8] "You look," said Ustaz Ramzi, "like someone who has been missing the ground." He set down the can. "Come. These beans need picking, and my back is older than the rest of me."
[9] She did not mean to stay. She meant to pick the beans out of politeness and go back down to the heat and her silent complaints. But the beans led to the tomatoes, which needed tying, and the tomatoes led to the basil, which he showed her how to pinch so that it grew outward instead of up, and by the time the call to the sunset prayer rose from a dozen minarets at once, the sky above the roof had turned the colour of apricots and she had forgotten, for almost an hour, to be unhappy.
[10] Before she left, he broke a stem from the basil and wrapped its cut end in a damp scrap of newspaper. "Put this in water," he said. "In a week it will have roots. Then it will need a tin of its own."
[11] Nour carried the stem down five flights of stairs as carefully as if it had been an egg. That night she set it in a glass on the windowsill, and in the morning, before anyone else was awake, she looked out of the window again. The walls of the well were still there. But now, along the tops of three or four buildings she had never properly noticed, she could make out other shapes against the brightening sky: the dark leaves of a fig, a line of pots, a vine spilling over a parapet. The city, it seemed, had gardens. They had simply been above her, where she had not thought to look.
questions.q: Which choice best summarises the passage?
c: A girl who is unhappy after moving to the city discovers, through an elderly neighbour's rooftop garden, that the city holds more green life than she had realised.
A girl persuades her parents to return to their village after she finds life in the city too hot and crowded.
A retired teacher helps a new neighbour with her geography lessons in return for help with his garden.
A girl and the caretaker's boy compete to see who can grow the best plants on the roof of their building.
questions.e: Nour begins homesick and shut in, meets Ustaz Ramzi among his plants, and ends by noticing gardens on other roofs. She never persuades her parents to leave, so the "return to the village" summary contradicts the story.
ce: Correct: it covers her unhappiness, the roof garden and her new view of the city.
Nour never asks to go back; the story ends with her seeing the city more hopefully.
Ramzi was a geography teacher, but he never helps Nour with lessons.
The caretaker's boy only tells her about the roof; there is no competition.

c: came to rest

**Passage 3 (Science).** This passage is adapted from an original article about corals in the Red Sea. The experiment described is fictional, and its data are for practice only.
**The Corals That Can Take the Heat**
[1] A coral reef may look like a garden of stone, but each coral is an animal, and most reef-building corals depend on a partnership. Inside their tissues live tiny algae that, like plants, use sunlight to make food. The algae share much of that food with the coral, which in return gives them shelter. The algae are also what give many corals their colour.
[2] The partnership has a weakness: heat. When the water stays only a little warmer than usual for several weeks, the relationship begins to break down, and the coral expels the algae living inside it. Without them, its tissue becomes almost transparent, and the white skeleton shows through. This is known as bleaching. A bleached coral is not yet dead, and if the water cools in time, the algae may return. But if the heat lasts too long, the coral may starve. As ocean temperatures have risen, mass bleaching has struck reefs in many parts of the world.
[3] Some corals in the northern Red Sea, however, seem unusually tough. Researchers have reported that corals in the Gulf of Aqaba, at the sea's northern end, can tolerate water several degrees warmer than the summer temperatures they normally experience. One explanation that scientists have proposed concerns the history of the sea itself. To reach the north after the last ice age, the ancestors of these corals would have had to pass through the warm, shallow waters of the far south. Only heat-tolerant corals, the argument goes, could have made the journey.
[4] To test this idea further, a team led by marine biologist Hana Saleh collected small fragments of the same coral species from two regions: reefs in the far north of the Red Sea and reefs in the far south. The fragments were placed in separate tanks and kept for three weeks at different temperatures, each a set number of degrees above the usual summer maximum for the reef where the fragments had been collected. At the end of the experiment, the team counted how many fragments had bleached. The results are shown in the table.
Table: Percentage of coral fragments bleached after three weeks
Temperature above usual summer maximum | Northern fragments bleached (%) | Southern fragments bleached (%)
0 °C | 0 | 2
+1 °C | 3 | 18
+2 °C | 8 | 47
+3 °C | 21 | 85
[5] The difference between the two groups grew as the water warmed. At the usual summer maximum, almost no fragments from either region bleached. At three degrees above it, however, most of the southern fragments had bleached, while about four in five of the northern fragments had not. "The northern corals are not immune to heat," Saleh says. "But they have a much larger safety margin than their southern relatives."
[6] Saleh is careful not to overstate the results. Fragments kept in tanks for a few weeks may not behave exactly like whole colonies on a living reef, where currents, sunlight and disease also play a part. And the study shows only that the northern corals tolerate heat better; it does not prove why. "Our data fit the idea that the journey north selected for tough corals," she says, "but other explanations are still possible."
[7] If the pattern holds, its importance could reach far beyond the Red Sea. Reefs in the Gulf of Aqaba may become a refuge where corals survive the warming of coming decades, and they may help scientists understand what makes some corals stronger than others. Even so, Saleh warns, heat is not the only danger reefs face. Pollution, careless coastal building and overfishing can harm even the toughest coral, and a reef that survives the heat may still be lost to other threats.

questions.p:
**Passage 4 (Paired texts).** Text 1 and Text 2 are original opinion pieces about how space should be explored.
**Text 1**
[1] Robots have taught us a great deal about the solar system. Rovers have crawled across the plains of Mars, and probes have flown past every planet. Yet anyone who has watched a rover at work knows how slow it is. Because radio signals take several minutes, and sometimes more than twenty, to travel between Earth and Mars, a rover cannot be driven like a remote-controlled car. Its team on Earth must plan each short drive in advance and then wait to discover what happened. A human geologist standing on the same ground could do in an afternoon what a rover does in weeks.
[2] Speed is not the only advantage people bring. A trained explorer notices the unexpected: an oddly coloured rock, a layer of sediment that does not fit the pattern, a clue that no one thought to program a machine to look for. Many of the greatest discoveries in science have come from exactly this kind of curiosity, the ability to change plans in the moment because something seems strange.
[3] Finally, human exploration inspires in a way that machines cannot. A photograph from a rover is fascinating; a footprint in the dust of another world is unforgettable. Crewed missions are expensive and risky, and no one should pretend otherwise. But a civilisation that sends only machines to the frontier has decided, in a quiet way, that the frontier is not really for people.
**Text 2**
[1] The dream of astronauts walking on Mars is a powerful one, and it is easy to see why. But when we ask what will produce the most knowledge for the money and effort spent, the answer is clear: robots.
[2] A human crew needs air, water, food, protection from radiation and, above all, a way home. Every one of these needs adds weight, cost and risk to a mission. A robot needs none of them. For the price of a single crewed landing, space agencies could send many robotic missions, to many different places, each equipped with instruments designed for a particular task. Some could drill beneath the ice of distant moons, where no astronaut could safely go; others could spend years watching a single planet's weather.
[3] It is often said that robots are slow and unimaginative. They are certainly slower than a person on foot. But they do not have to return home, and so they can stay at work far longer than any crew. Some rovers sent to Mars have kept working for years after their planned missions ended. And the curiosity that guides them belongs to people after all: the scientists on Earth who study every image and decide where to go next.
[4] None of this means that people should never travel beyond the Moon. Perhaps one day they will, when the technology is safer and cheaper. For now, though, the wisest course is to let machines go first, and to send them in great numbers.

crewed missions are cheap and carry very little risk.
sending people to explore other worlds offers advantages that robots cannot provide.
robots should no longer be sent to explore the solar system.

Text 1 admits that crewed missions are "expensive and risky".

questions.p:
**Passage 5 (Science).** This passage is adapted from an original article about the problem of debris in orbit around the Earth.
**Crowded Skies**
[1] When the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 in 1957, the space around the Earth was empty of human-made objects. Today it is anything but. Thousands of working satellites now circle the planet, carrying telephone calls, television signals, weather data and the navigation signals that guide drivers through unfamiliar cities. Alongside them travel many thousands more objects that do no useful work at all: dead satellites, the spent upper stages of rockets, and fragments left behind by explosions and collisions. Together, this material is known as space debris.
[2] At first glance, the danger may seem small. Space is vast, and most pieces of debris are tiny. But objects in low orbit travel at around 28,000 kilometres per hour, many times faster than a bullet. At such speeds, even a fragment no larger than a coin can strike with enough energy to damage a satellite, and a larger piece could destroy one. The International Space Station, which carries a crew, has had to move out of the way of approaching debris on a number of occasions.
[3] The most worrying feature of the problem is that it can feed on itself. In 1978, a NASA scientist named Donald Kessler described a possible chain reaction. When two objects collide, they break into hundreds or thousands of fragments, each of which can cause further collisions. If the number of objects in a crowded orbit passed a certain point, Kessler argued, collisions could continue on their own, even if no new satellites were ever launched. In the worst case, some orbits might become too dangerous to use for many years.
[4] For a long time, this scenario seemed largely theoretical. Then, in 2009, an inactive Russian satellite and a working American communications satellite collided above Siberia, scattering clouds of debris. It was the first known accidental collision between two whole satellites, and it showed that Kessler's warning was not merely a thought experiment.
[5] Engineers and space agencies are now working on the problem from two directions. The first is prevention. Satellites can be designed to move themselves into lower orbits at the end of their working lives, where the thin upper atmosphere slowly drags them down until they burn up. Some carry small sails that unfold to increase this drag and speed up their fall. Rocket stages can be made to vent their leftover fuel so that they do not later explode. The second direction is cleanup. Several experimental missions have tested ways of capturing debris, using nets, harpoons, magnets or robotic arms, so that it can be pulled down into the atmosphere.

Then, in 2009, an inactive Russian satellite and a working American communications satellite collided above Siberia, scattering clouds of debris. It was the first known accidental collision between two whole satellites, and it showed that Kessler's warning was not merely a thought experiment.
[5] Engineers and space agencies are now working on the problem from two directions. The first is prevention. Satellites can be designed to move themselves into lower orbits at the end of their working lives, where the thin upper atmosphere slowly drags them down until they burn up. Some carry small sails that unfold to increase this drag and speed up their fall. Rocket stages can be made to vent their leftover fuel so that they do not later explode. The second direction is cleanup. Several experimental missions have tested ways of capturing debris, using nets, harpoons, magnets or robotic arms, so that it can be pulled down into the atmosphere.
[6] Neither approach is simple. Cleaning up even a single large object is expensive, and there are no easy rules for deciding who should pay to remove a piece of debris that belongs to another country or to a company that no longer exists. Prevention is cheaper, but it works only if satellite operators around the world follow the same rules.
[7] The orbits around the Earth, in other words, are a shared resource, much like the oceans or the air. They can be used by everyone, and they can be spoiled by anyone. Whether they remain useful for future generations will depend less on any single invention than on the willingness of nations and companies to treat them with care.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the author's view in the final paragraph?
c: Orbits belong to the countries that launched the first satellites.
Keeping Earth's orbits usable depends mainly on cooperation and responsible behaviour.
A single new invention will soon solve the problem of space debris.
The oceans and the air are more important to protect than orbits.
questions.e: The author calls orbits "a shared resource" and says their future depends "less on any single invention than on the willingness of nations and companies to treat them with care". That sentence directly rejects the idea of one invention solving the problem.
ce: The author says orbits "can be used by everyone".
Correct: the future of orbits depends on care and cooperation.
The author says the answer depends less on any single invention.
The oceans and air are used as a comparison, not ranked above orbits.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the explanation for every question, including the ones you got right; a lucky guess is not a skill yet.
Write down the skill tag of every question you missed (for example Punctuation, Transitions, Inference or Data and graphics) and count which tags appear most often. Those are your weak skills.

For Literacy Test 1 mistakes, go back to "EST Literacy Test 1: Writing and Language" and open the lesson for each weak skill from its table "Where each skill is fully taught on this site" (for example Sentence Boundaries, Commas and Extra Information, Transitions, Concision and Redundancy, Relevance: Add, Delete and Writer's Goal, Organisation: Order and Transitions, Word Choice and Tone).

For Literacy Test 2 mistakes, go back to "EST Literacy Test 2: Reading" and its lesson table (for example Central Ideas and Details, Inferences, Words in Context, Text Structure and Purpose, Command of Evidence: Textual, Command of Evidence: Quantitative, Cross-Text Connections).

If you ran out of time, reread the pacing plans on the two guide pages and "The EST Explained", then retake this test later with the timer on, or try a Digital SAT or ACT practice test on this site for extra timed practice.
